v.why: Adding a 3x3 conv where edge 3 was empty gives much larger gains than replacing an existing op (exps 1,5,7,8 vs 2-4).
Creating a direct input-output path is far more valuable when none existed (exps 71,75,77,80 vs 72-74,76).
Replacing the strongest op on edge 3 with a parameter-free skip loses capacity (exps 73,78 negative vs positive otherwise).
Removing a 3x3 conv on edge 0 costs far more than removing a 1x1, skip, or pool (exps 22,30 vs 21,23,24).
Deleting a 3x3 conv on node2->node3 consistently hurts more than deleting skip/1x1 (exps 62,65-70 vs 61,63).
Replacing a 3x3 conv on edge 4 with skip loses substantial accuracy, unlike replacing other ops (exps 43,50 vs 41,42).
Downgrading 3x3 to 1x1 on edge 1 is clearly harmful while replacing none/skip is neutral or positive (exp 54 vs 51,52).
Swapping a 3x3 conv for pooling on edge 2 is negative while replacing weaker ops is neutral-to-positive (exps 34,39 vs 31-33).
Without a direct input-output edge, the node2->node3 path carries more of the signal, so upgrading it matters more (exp 15 vs 16).
When the cell already has a 3x3 conv on the input-output edge, adding another 3x3 gives diminishing returns (exps 87,90 vs 81-86).

raw:
Each hypothesis below rests on the conditioned and unconditioned cases in the 100 experiments, plus the general pattern that a 3x3 conv usually beats 1x1, skip or pool in this space. Most have only one to four supporting experiments, so treat them as likely, not confirmed.

1. **Edge 3 → nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 3 is none.** When edge 3 was none, gains were large (experiments 1, 5, 7, 8: up to +25 on ImageNet16-120). When edge 3 already had an operation, gains were smaller (2–4).
2. **Edge 3 → skip_connect helps more when edge 3 is none.** Adding a direct input-to-output path gave big gains (71, 75, 77, 80) versus small or negative ones (72–74, 76). Experiment 79 is a counterexample: in an all-avg_pool cell the same edit lost about 18 points on CIFAR.
3. **Edge 3 → skip_connect helps less when edge 3 is nor_conv_3x3.** Replacing a 3x3 conv was negative or roughly zero (73, 78), while replacing other operations was mostly positive.
4. **Edge 0 → none hurts more when edge 0 is nor_conv_3x3.** Removing a 3x3 conv cost much more (22, 30) than removing 1x1, skip or pool (21, 23, 24).
5. **Edge 5 → none hurts more when edge 5 is nor_conv_3x3.** Removing the 3x3 conv on node 2 → 3 consistently cost more (62, 65–70) than removing skip or 1x1 (61, 63).
6. **Edge 4 → skip_connect hurts more when edge 4 is nor_conv_3x3.** Losing a 3x3 conv here was strongly negative (43, 50), versus roughly zero for other operations (41, 42).
7. **Edge 1 → nor_conv_1x1 hurts more when edge 1 is nor_conv_3x3.** Downgrading a 3x3 conv to 1x1 was clearly negative (54), unlike replacing none or skip (51, 52).
8. **Edge 2 → avg_pool_3x3 hurts more when edge 2 is nor_conv_3x3.** Replacing a 3x3 conv was negative (34, 39), while replacing none, skip or 1x1 was neutral to positive on ImageNet16-120 (31–33).
9. **Edge 5 → nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 3 is none.** Without a direct input-to-output edge, the node 2 → 3 path carries the signal, so upgrading it gained more (15 vs. 16).
10. **Edge 0 → nor_conv_3x3 helps less when edge 3 is nor_conv_3x3.** Once the cell already has a 3x3 conv on the input-to-output edge, adding another gave much smaller gains (87, 90 vs. 81–86).
